conditions.name: Tension-type headache

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: The commonest headache: a dull, pressing band around the head, mild to moderate, with no nausea and no aversion to light, and not made worse by walking about.
workup: Simple analgesia, limited to avoid rebound

exam.step: Assess range of movement and crepitus

exam.positive: A hot joint suggests an inflammatory or septic cause

labs.test: Clinical diagnosis over 45 with typical features
labs.confirms: No test needed if the picture is typical

labs.test: X-ray only if the diagnosis is uncertain
labs.confirms: Joint space loss, osteophytes, sclerosis, cysts

conditions.name: Osteoarthritis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Cartilage wear in weight-bearing joints. Pain worsens with use through the day, morning stiffness lasts under half an hour, and the joint is bony rather than hot.
workup: Clinical diagnosis over 45 with typical features

exam.positive: Reproduces radicular arm symptoms if a root is involved

labs.confirms: Imaging finds age-related change in most adults

labs.test: MRI cervical spine only if myelopathy or radiculopathy

conditions.name: Cervicogenic headache

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Headache referred from the neck joints. One-sided, starting at the back of the head and spreading forward, provoked by neck posture or movement.

exam.step: Ask specifically about a sudden deceleration injury (road traffic collision, fall)
exam.positive: The defining precipitant -- absence of one should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Check for arm weakness, numbness, or midline cervical spine tenderness after significant trauma
exam.positive: Any of these need imaging to exclude a fracture or cord injury before labelling this simple whiplash

exam.step: Apply a validated clinical decision rule (e.g. Canadian C-spine rule)
exam.positive: Determines objectively whether imaging is needed, rather than imaging everyone or no one

labs.confirms: Validated decision rule for whether imaging is needed -- avoids both over- and under-investigation
Excludes fracture or instability when red flags or the clinical rule indicate it

conditions.name: Whiplash injury

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Neck pain and stiffness developing hours to a day after a sudden deceleration injury -- classically a road traffic collision -- sometimes with headache or arm symptoms. Road-traffic-collision rates and injury patterns are high in India, so this is worth considering explicitly given the volume of minor-collision neck injuries seen in routine practice. Neurological symptoms (arm weakness/numbness), or midline cervical spine tenderness after significant trauma, need imaging to exclude a fracture or cord injury before this is labelled simple whiplash.
workup: Clinical assessment against a validated rule (e.g. Canadian C-spine rule) to decide if imaging is needed
Plain X-ray/CT if red flags are present
Early mobilisation and physiotherapy -- genuinely better outcomes than prolonged collar immobilisation

exam.step: Ask specifically about a preceding injury, looking for its ABSENCE
exam.positive: Cervical spondylosis is a degenerative, NOT trauma-related, condition -- a clear preceding injury points to whiplash instead

exam.step: Assess range of neck movement and for stiffness, particularly first thing in the morning
exam.positive: Genuinely common findings, mirroring the classical description of Manyastambha (neck stiffness)

exam.step: Ask about arm numbness, tingling, or weakness
exam.positive: Suggests nerve root involvement (cervical radiculopathy) needing its own targeted assessment, though not universally present

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis and to guide initial management

labs.test: Plain X-ray or MRI cervical spine
labs.confirms: Reserved for significant/progressive neurological symptoms or when the diagnosis is unclear, not needed for typical, uncomplicated cases

conditions.name: Cervical spondylosis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Age-related degenerative wear of the cervical spine's discs and joints, causing chronic neck pain and stiffness, sometimes with arm numbness/tingling if a nerve root is affected -- genuinely very common with age, correlating with the classical Manyastambha (neck stiffness). Distinct from Whiplash Injury sharing this bundle: cervical spondylosis is degenerative, NOT trauma-related, and develops gradually over months to years rather than following an identifiable injury.
workup: Ask specifically about the ABSENCE of a preceding injury, and the gradual, longstanding nature of symptoms
Assess for arm numbness, tingling, or weakness suggesting nerve root involvement (cervical radiculopathy), which needs its own targeted assessment
Conservative management first-line: physiotherapy, neck-strengthening exercises, and simple analgesia -- effective for most people
MRI cervical spine if there are significant or progressive neurological symptoms (arm weakness, numbness, or any bladder/bowel involvement), rather than for pain alone

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
